name: Felix Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for anything. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at the North Gate housing site, cutting decking boards and helping set the timber stairs. I'm fifty-eight, still a junior because I came in after a long stretch delivering parcels; I left school early and the lead still checks my stair angles. My partner Ilse works at a small pharmacy, and our children are grown. The site rate is good and we've saved nearly a year's expenses. I use an AI tool now and then to read a drawing note, but only after someone on the crew has shown me it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a little software can make the timber order easier, provided the boards still arrive in the right lengths. The deck won't lay itself, so I would carry on as usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my own pay stays safe here, and Ilse's pharmacy hours are steady. We have enough saved for a long ordinary gap and several builders nearby, so I am not losing sleep over modest office changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep cutting decking with lead carpenter Bruno checking the unusual angles. In the first year I'd use the same drawing tool when he has checked it and keep the usual transfer to our savings account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel settled about this one. I would rather get the stair edge flush than spend the day talking about a software update.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would prove the drawing tool useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it picks out the correct stair rise from a real plan and Bruno gets the same number, it has earned a place in my pocket. I won't cut costly timber from an unverified screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you worry about being a junior at your age?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sometimes, when the younger workers finish a tricky corner faster. But the pay is good and I can learn from them while the work is here.

say: I'd accept **easier timber orders** when the lengths arrive right.
I'd say the **deck still needs hands** even with small software changes.
think: My site pay and Ilse's **pharmacy hours** look secure.
Nearly **one year saved** and nearby builders cover a normal gap.
do: Keep cutting **decking boards** with Bruno checking unusual angles.
Use a **verified drawing tool** and maintain the usual savings transfer.
feel: **Settled** about small changes, focused on finishing clean stair edges.
S0.quote: I won't cut costly timber from an unverified screen.
fieldNote: Felix accepts occasional AI help only after **Bruno's check** matches the drawing.
Good pay, Ilse's steady pharmacy hours and **nearly a year saved** make this mild path secure.

steps.text: Keep cutting decking boards at North Gate
Use the AI drawing tool only after Bruno verifies its measurements

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say faster buying might help, but a computer cannot see that a pile of boards was left in the rain. I would ask the foreman to show us how the next jobs are actually booked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the office needs fewer estimators, there may be a pause before new site contracts. I can work with the tools we already have, yet a junior worker might be sent home first when a firm waits for orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my North Gate shifts and ask Bruno which jobs are booked after this block. If the next site has no confirmed date, I'll visit the timber contractor down the road and another builder I know; I'd use the AI tool for plan notes only where it has already proved accurate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy, though our savings would carry a short pause. I don't want to change employers over a rumour, but I won't ignore an empty schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why visit the timber contractor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I delivered parcels there for years, and the owner knows I now do site carpentry. I would ask about paid hands-on work, not take a promise as a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say if the foreman showed a full schedule?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay with this builder and keep learning stairs from Bruno. A printed start date would calm me more than a general claim that AI creates opportunities.

say: I'd remind the crew **wet timber** still has to be checked in person.
I'd ask for **booked jobs** rather than a promise about software.
think: Fewer estimators might leave **contract gaps** on site.
My **junior place** could be vulnerable if the firm pauses hiring.
do: Keep **North Gate shifts** and ask Bruno for the next start date.
Visit **two local employers** if the next site is unconfirmed.
feel: **Uneasy** about an empty schedule, with savings to cover a short pause.
S1.quote: A printed start date would calm me more than a general claim that AI creates opportunities.
fieldNote: His fallback relies on a **known timber contractor**, connecting an old delivery route to possible paid work.
A confirmed start date would keep him at North Gate; he does not treat a **rumour** as a reason to move.

steps.text: Keep taking paid North Gate shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Bruno the 2028 thinking machine could plan the stairs before we touch timber, while robots that can build them arrive around 2031. I would want a real site demonstration and proper safety rules before working beside one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty, I may still earn cutting boards even if the office changes. At sixty-three, a robot could take the stair and decking work; Ilse's pay and our savings help, but losing my higher wage would change how soon we can retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll add extra from full paid weeks to savings and ask Bruno to show me a proven digital stair check. In 2029 I'll keep taking paid shifts; if the builder reduces junior hours, I'll apply to the local timber contractor and two site crews before our reserve starts falling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a genuine wage loss after 2031. I can still make calls, and I would rather look for paid work than assume the family will cover us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn robot maintenance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a paid apprenticeship with a real employer offered it, I would consider enrolling, but I wouldn't pay for a course on a sales pitch. I need to know what job follows the training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your grown children hear from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them what the builder has actually done to our hours. They have their own households, so I won't ask them to replace my wage.

say: I'd separate **2028 planning** from 2031 hands-on robots.
I'd ask for a **real safety demonstration** before site use.
think: At **sixty-three**, robots could take my stair and decking hours.
Ilse's wage and our **reserve** may not replace my higher pay.
do: Save extra from **full weeks** and check a proven digital stair tool.
Apply to local timber and **site crews** if junior hours fall.
feel: **Anxious** about a large wage loss, with applications available.
S2.quote: I need to know what job follows the training.
fieldNote: Felix puts the main income threat at the **robot date**, after a period of continued hands-on work.
His interest in an apprenticeship is **conditional on pay** and a real employer, while his immediate plan is to apply elsewhere.

steps.text: Save extra after full paid site weeks
Use Bruno’s proven digital stair check on paid work
Keep taking paid site shifts in 2029
Apply to local timber and site crews if junior hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us look at machines on a real job and decide which training earns its cost. I would want the builder to give workers notice before changing the roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-three when thinking AI changes planning and sixty-six when robots could do the site work. Ilse and I may be able to retire around then, but we haven't counted the full cost of living without my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll stay on paid decking jobs, save more from good months and ask Bruno for copies of completed stair sheets. In 2032 I'd take available site shifts and compare a tested digital checker with the plan; if the firm later empties my schedule, I'd apply to nearby contractors while I still have recent work to show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more room to decide than in the fast case. I am still wary of a glossy demonstration, but five years gives me time to see a machine earn its place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What goes into your retirement calculation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ilse and I need to list actual bills, savings and income that continues after our wages end. I don't know the pension figure well enough to promise anything today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop working at sixty-six?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the numbers allow it and my knees are tired, perhaps. If not, I would look for paid lighter carpentry instead of pretending the calendar can pay rent.

say: I'd ask for **real site evidence** before paying for training.
I'd insist on **roster notice** before machines replace shifts.
think: At **sixty-six**, robots may meet an unsettled retirement plan.
We need **actual income figures** before I can stop earning.
do: Keep **decking shifts** and save from good months.
Compare a **tested checker** with the stair plan in 2032.
Apply to **nearby contractors** if the schedule empties.
feel: More **room to decide**, while untested claims still bother me.
S3.quote: I don't know the pension figure well enough to promise anything today.
fieldNote: The five-year window lets Felix gather **completed stair sheets** and real income figures.
He avoids assuming retirement, and would seek **paid lighter work** if the household numbers still require earnings.

steps.text: Keep taking paid decking work in 2032
Save extra after strong site months
Use a tested digital checker against the stair plan
Apply to nearby contractors if site work dries up

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives us time to finish the work and teach apprentices how to judge a board before cutting it. I would still ask for safety proof if robots come onto sites in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-eight, thinking AI may do the plans, and at seventy-one robots may handle the decking. I could be retired by then, but I might still need paid small repairs if our savings and Ilse's income are not enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking full site weeks and putting extra into savings while the rate is good. In 2037 I'd accept paid ground-level repair jobs if needed and sit with Ilse to compare actual bills with our income before I finally leave the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the far-off technology. My knees and the quality of the boards on today's lorry are closer to hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children help if money was short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They would offer, because we are close, but they have families of their own. I would ask their company before I asked for their wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach a new apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd teach the apprentice to sort twisted boards before measuring a stair. A straight line on paper will not straighten wet wood.

say: I'd use the decade to **teach apprentices** how to judge timber.
I'd still ask for **robot safety proof** in 2039.
think: At **sixty-eight**, I may still want paid small repairs.
At **seventy-one**, stopping depends on savings and Ilse's real income.
do: Keep **full site weeks** and save extra while pay is strong.
Take **ground-level repairs** in 2037 if wages are needed.
Compare **bills and income** with Ilse before leaving paid work.
feel: **Calm** about distant robots, focused on knees and present timber.
S4.quote: A straight line on paper will not straighten wet wood.
fieldNote: Felix views the decade as **working and teaching time**, while leaving paid repairs open.
He keeps grown children's wages outside the budget and puts **retirement figures** ahead of a calendar date.

steps.text: Keep taking paid site weeks while fit
Save extra after full paid months

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because robots could reach decking by sixty-three, when I may still need the higher site wage. Clear notice, a safe trial and actual paid openings at local contractors would make the change easier to face.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who pays for a board cut wrong by a machine. A builder should count wasted timber and the worker's time before calling a system cheaper.

headlineQuote: A builder should count wasted timber and the worker's time before calling a system cheaper.
portrait: Felix is a **fifty-eight-year-old junior** site carpenter after years delivering parcels.
His higher pay, Ilse's pharmacy wage and **nearly a year saved** give him a solid reserve.
He uses AI **occasionally**, after a trusted carpenter verifies its drawing numbers.
He favours **paid work and apprenticeship** while refusing to guess at retirement income.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** could remove his decking hours when site robots arrive around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **clear notice**, safe machine trials and paid local contractor openings.
